title: Conv+BN+ReLU Operator Fusion
description: Fusing convolution, batch normalization, and ReLU into a single kernel removes two memory round-trips per layer. The pass matches the pattern in the high-level graph IR, folds batch-norm statistics into the convolution weights offline, and emits one fused operator for the backend. This typically cuts inference latency by 15 to 40 percent on CNNs and is a standard pass in compilers such as XLA, TensorRT, and TVM.

demo.code:
ops = [("conv", 12.4), ("bn", 3.2), ("relu", 1.1)]
total = sum(t for _, t in ops)
print("before fusion: %d launches, %.1f ms" % (len(ops), total))
print("after fusion: 1 launch, %.1f ms" % (total * 0.62))
print("latency saved: %.1f ms" % (total - total * 0.62))

title: Post-Training INT8 Quantization Pass
description: This pass converts a trained FP32 model to INT8 by inserting quantize and dequantize nodes and calibrating activation ranges on a small sample of real inputs. Min-max or KL-divergence calibration picks per-tensor scales, and sensitive layers can be kept in FP16 through a mixed-precision policy. The result is roughly 4x smaller models and 2-3x faster inference on integer-capable hardware with accuracy loss usually under one percent.

demo.code:
import math
fp32 = [0.13, -1.42, 2.718, 0.0, 3.99]
scale = max(abs(x) for x in fp32) / 127.0
q = [round(x / scale) for x in fp32]
dq = [v * scale for v in q]
mse = sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(fp32, dq)) / len(fp32)
print("scale:", round(scale, 5))
print("quantized:", q)
print("mse after round-trip:", round(mse, 6))

title: TVM AutoTVM Schedule Search
description: AutoTVM searches the space of loop schedules for each tensor operator, measuring real hardware latency for candidate schedules. It uses a learned cost model to prune the search space, then tunes the top candidates on-device. This turns hand-written kernel expertise into an automated pass that routinely beats vendor libraries on new accelerators.

demo.code:
trials = {"tile_8x8": 14.2, "tile_16x16": 9.7, "tile_32x4": 11.3, "tile_16x32": 8.1}
best = min(trials, key=trials.get)
print("trials measured:", len(trials))
print("best schedule:", best, "->", trials[best], "ms")
print("speedup vs worst: %.2fx" % (max(trials.values()) / trials[best]))

title: XLA Algebraic Simplifier
description: XLA's algebraic simplifier applies rewrite rules such as x+0=x, reshape-of-reshape folding, and broadcast elimination at the HLO level. These cheap local rewrites shrink the graph before expensive passes run, and they are semantics-preserving by construction. Dozens of such rules compose into a surprisingly large cumulative win.

title: MLIR Progressive Lowering Pipeline
description: MLIR lowers a model through a stack of dialects: high-level tensor ops to linalg, then to affine loops, then to LLVM IR. Each level applies its own optimizations before lowering further, so domain knowledge is preserved as long as possible. This progressive approach lets one infrastructure target CPUs, GPUs, and custom accelerators from the same frontend.

demo.code:
levels = ["tensor", "linalg", "affine", "scf", "llvm"]
op = "matmul(tensor<4x4xf32>)"
for i, lv in enumerate(levels):
    print("level %d [%s]: %s" % (i, lv, op))
    op = op.replace("tensor", lv, 1)
print("final:", op)

title: TensorRT Layer Precision Calibration
description: TensorRT's builder calibrates each layer's dynamic range with a representative dataset, choosing per-layer INT8 or FP16 precision under an accuracy budget. Layers that lose too much accuracy stay in FP32 while the rest quantize, producing a mixed-precision engine. The calibration cache can be reused so rebuilds are fast.

t: GPU Memory Planner with Liveness Analysis
title: GPU Memory Planner with Liveness Analysis
description: The memory planner computes tensor liveness intervals across the execution schedule and reuses buffers whose lifetimes do not overlap. This turns naive per-tensor allocation into a compact plan that often halves peak memory. Static planning matters most on memory-constrained edge GPUs where fragmentation would otherwise cause out-of-memory failures.

title: CPU Vectorization via Loop Tiling
description: For CPU backends the compiler tiles loops to fit L1 cache and emits SIMD vector instructions for the inner loop. Tile sizes are tuned per microarchitecture, and remainder loops handle non-multiple dimensions. Good tiling plus vectorization is often the difference between a 2x and a 10x speedup over naive loops.

demo.code:
N, TILE, VEC = 1000, 64, 8
tiles = (N + TILE - 1) // TILE
vec_iters = TILE // VEC
print("elements:", N, "tiles:", tiles, "vector iters per tile:", vec_iters)
print("estimated ops with SIMD: %d (vs %d scalar)" % (N // VEC, N))

title: Dynamic Shape Recompilation Guard
description: Models with dynamic batch or sequence length recompile whenever a new shape appears, which can stall serving. The guard pass buckets shapes into a small set of compiled variants and inserts cheap runtime shape checks that dispatch to the right variant. This bounds the number of compiled programs while keeping dynamic models fast.

title: Operator Fallback Partitioning
description: When a backend cannot compile every operator, the partitioner splits the graph into supported subgraphs compiled natively and unsupported ops that fall back to a reference runtime. Cut points are chosen to minimize data transfer across the boundary. This lets new hardware ship useful compilers long before full operator coverage exists.

demo.code:
ops = ["conv", "relu", "custom_op", "add", "weird_norm", "matmul"]
supported = {"conv", "relu", "add", "matmul"}
native = [o for o in ops if o in supported]
fallback = [o for o in ops if o not in supported]
print("native:", native)
print("fallback:", fallback)
print("boundary crossings:", len(fallback))

title: Gradient Checkpointing Insertion
description: Checkpointing trades compute for memory by discarding intermediate activations in the forward pass and recomputing them during backprop. The compiler inserts checkpoint markers at segment boundaries chosen to balance the recompute cost. This lets very deep models train on GPUs that could never hold the full activation set.
benefit: Train deeper models in less memory

demo.code:
layers, seg = 24, 6
checkpoints = list(range(0, layers, seg))
mem_full = layers * 100
mem_ckpt = (seg + len(checkpoints)) * 100
print("checkpoints at layers:", checkpoints)
print("memory full: %d MB -> checkpointed: %d MB" % (mem_full, mem_ckpt))
print("recompute overhead: ~%.0f%%" % (100.0 * seg / layers))

title: Sparse Tensor Compiler Support
description: Sparse compilers represent tensors in formats like CSR and generate code that skips zero elements instead of multiplying them. Format selection, reordering, and merge-lattice code generation turn sparsity into real speedups for pruned models and graph workloads. Without compiler support, sparse data structures stay slower than dense ones despite doing less math.

demo.code:
dense = [0, 0, 3.5, 0, 0, -1.2, 0, 0, 0, 7.7]
csr_vals = [v for v in dense if v != 0]
csr_idx = [i for i, v in enumerate(dense) if v != 0]
print("dense nnz skipped:", len(dense) - len(csr_vals), "of", len(dense))
x = 2.0
print("sparse dot:", sum(v * x for v in csr_vals))

title: Kernel Autotuning Database
description: The compiler keeps a database of measured kernel timings keyed by operator, shapes, dtype, and device. At compile time it queries the database instead of re-tuning, so the second compile of a similar model is nearly instant. Entries age out and re-tune when driver versions change.

demo.code:
db = {("conv", (1, 64, 56, 56)): ("tile16", 8.1), ("gemm", (512, 512)): ("tile32", 3.3)}
key = ("conv", (1, 64, 56, 56))
print("cache hit:", key in db, "->", db.get(key))
print("entries:", len(db))

title: NPU Systolic Array Mapping
description: Mapping matmul onto a systolic array means tiling the operands so data flows through the array with minimal DRAM traffic. The compiler picks tile sizes from the array dimensions and double-buffers weights while activations stream. Good mapping is what separates an NPU's paper TOPS from its delivered TOPS.

demo.code:
ARRAY = 128
M = N = K = 512
tiles = (M // ARRAY) * (N // ARRAY)
macs = M * N * K
print("tiles on 128x128 array:", tiles)
print("total MACs: %d  array MACs/cycle: %d" % (macs, ARRAY * ARRAY))
print("compute cycles: %d" % (macs // (ARRAY * ARRAY)))

title: Control-Flow to Dataflow Conversion
description: Models with data-dependent control flow are hard to compile, so the pass converts simple branches into select/mask operations over tensors. Where conversion is impossible it outlines the branch into a separate compiled function with a runtime dispatch. This keeps dynamic models compilable without giving up on static optimization of the straight-line parts.

demo.code:
def branch(x, use_a):
    return x * 2 if use_a else x + 10
xs = [1, 2, 3, 4]
mask = [True, False, True, False]
flat = [x * 2 if m else x + 10 for x, m in zip(xs, mask)]
print("branched:", [branch(x, m) for x, m in zip(xs, mask)])
print("flattened:", flat)

title: Cross-Device Pipeline Partitioning
description: For multi-device serving the compiler slices the model into stages and assigns each stage to a device, inserting send/recv pairs at the cuts. Micro-batching keeps all devices busy and the partitioner balances stage latencies to avoid bubbles. This is how single models scale across GPUs that cannot hold the whole model.
benefit: Serve models bigger than one device

demo.code:
stage_ms = [12, 11, 13, 12]
micro = 4
bubble = max(stage_ms) * (len(stage_ms) - 1)
steady = max(stage_ms) * micro
print("stage times:", stage_ms)
print("throughput ms/microbatch: %.1f" % (steady / micro))
print("pipeline efficiency: %.1f%%" % (100 * steady / (steady + bubble)))

title: Dead Code Elimination for Graphs
description: Training graphs accumulate dead branches, unused auxiliary outputs, and stale control dependencies. DCE walks from the fetch nodes backwards and drops everything unreachable, which also removes the memory those tensors would have held. It runs late in the pipeline so earlier passes can create new dead code safely.

title: FP16 Loss Scaling Codegen
description: Mixed-precision training needs loss scaling to keep small gradients representable in FP16. The compiler inserts scale multiply before backward and unscale plus overflow checks after, fusing them with the optimizer step where possible. Dynamic scaling adjusts the factor automatically when overflow is detected.

demo.code:
scale = 1024.0
grads = [1e-6, 2e-5, 0.0, 3e-4]
scaled = [g * scale for g in grads]
overflow = any(abs(g) > 65504 for g in scaled)
print("scaled grads:", scaled)
print("overflow:", overflow, "-> new scale:", scale / 2 if overflow else scale * 2)

title: Profile-Guided Layout Selection
description: The compiler profiles tensor layouts (NCHW vs NHWC vs blocked) on the target device and bakes the fastest choice into the compiled artifact. Layout transforms are inserted only where the profile says they pay off. This beats any fixed heuristic because the best layout genuinely differs between GPUs, CPUs, and NPUs.

demo.code:
timings = {"NCHW": 22.4, "NHWC": 18.9, "NCHWc8": 15.2}
best = min(timings, key=timings.get)
print("layout timings:", timings)
print("selected:", best, "->", timings[best], "ms")
print("speedup vs default NCHW: %.2fx" % (timings["NCHW"] / timings[best]))

title: Ahead-of-Time Compilation Cache
description: AOT compilation is slow, so the compiler hashes the graph, shapes, flags, and compiler version into a cache key and reuses previously built artifacts. Cache hits skip minutes of compilation in CI and deployment pipelines. Invalidation is conservative: any flag change busts the entry.

demo.code:
import hashlib
def key(graph, flags, ver):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    h.update((graph + flags + ver).encode())
    return h.hexdigest()[:12]
cache = {}
k = key("resnet50", "O2", "v3")
cache[k] = "resnet50_o2_v3.so"
print("cache key:", k, "hit:", k in cache)
